task.question: Suppose r orthonormal real columns are placed at r distinct positions among the N columns of an orthogonal matrix, and suppose r < N so at least one column position is left free. The naive completion to an orthogonal matrix may land in the reflection family (determinant -1) rather than the rotation family (determinant +1). Prove that one can always repair the orientation so the final matrix has determinant exactly +1 while leaving every one of the r prescribed columns completely unchanged. Explain why the strict inequality r < N is exactly what makes the repair possible, and why the repair cannot in general be done when r = N.
assumptions: an orthogonal completion with the prescribed columns exists
r < N so at least one column is unused
conventions: sign flip is a diagonal matrix with a single -1 entry

cases.worked_derivation:
Let V be the prescribed columns and e their injective placement. Take an orthogonal completion U, so UᵀU=I and U(i,e(a))=V(i,a). Taking determinants gives det(U)²=1, hence det(U)=±1. If det(U)=1, retain U.

If det(U)=-1, the inequality r<N implies that e is not surjective: surjectivity would force N≤r. Choose j outside its image and set S=diag(s), where s(j)=-1 and s(k)=1 for k≠j. Then SᵀS=I and det(S)=-1. Thus (US)ᵀ(US)=Sᵀ(UᵀU)S=I and det(US)=(-1)(-1)=1. Right multiplication rescales columns, so (US)(i,e(a))=U(i,e(a)) because e(a)≠j. Every prescribed column is unchanged.

The strict inequality guarantees a repair for every input, rather than being necessary for each individual successful frame. For r=N>0 prescribe V=diag(-1,1,…,1) in all positions. Any matrix preserving all columns must equal V, whose determinant is -1; therefore an SO(N) completion is impossible. If the fully prescribed frame already has determinant +1, it of course needs no repair. At N=1 this is the scalar frame [-1]; with r=0 the completion [1] works. At N=0 there is no r<N and the unique empty matrix has determinant +1, so the reflection obstruction has no zero-dimensional instance.

task.question:
Let sigma be a bijection of the N physical wires, sigma:Fin N equiv Fin N. Its INDUCED bitstring bijection is R_sigma(b)(w)=b(sigma^{-1}(w)); define P by P|b>=|R_sigma(b)>. Thus P is specifically this wire-induced basis permutation, not an arbitrary permutation of all2^N computational labels. A primitive circuit has chronological matrices U_1,...,U_t, with first-listed gate acting first. Consistently rename each gate's target and each control by sigma, retaining gate kind and angle.

Prove that the renamed circuit realizes P(U_t...U_1)P^{-1}, rather than insertion of a one-sided physical permutation. Justify the single-gate conjugation from the induced bitstring action and show the interior inverse/permutation cancellations through the chronological product. Explain why output-only relabeling fails to preserve products, giving two identity stages and an actual nontrivial involutive wire swap as a witness when N>=2. Include empty circuit and N=0,1 boundaries. Finally assess why the same wire-renaming assertion would be false if P were an arbitrary unrelated basis-label permutation: on one wire compare P=X with a nonzero RY. Distinguish algebraic basis reindexing from a physical SWAP/routing implementation; no hardware routing cost follows for free.

cases.worked_derivation:
Write Rσ(b)(w)=b(σ⁻¹(w)) and P|b⟩=|Rσ(b)⟩. Then Rσ(b)(σ(w))=b(w). Hence target bits, control tests, and equality of all spectator bits are transported by the same wire bijection. Renaming an X or CX gate transports its bit action; renaming RY or RZ retains the same local 2×2 matrix and angle. For each primitive U′P=PU on every basis ket, so U′=PUP⁻¹. In entries, (PMP⁻¹)(a,b)=M(a∘σ,b∘σ), exactly the source reindexing map.

The chronological product multiplies later gates on the left. Therefore U′t⋯U′1=(PUtP⁻¹)⋯(PU1P⁻¹)=P(Ut⋯U1)P⁻¹; the interior P⁻¹P pairs are identities. Equivalently, two-sided reindexing is multiplicative, so induction on the chronological list proves the same identity. The empty list denotes I and PIP⁻¹=I. For N=0 or 1 every wire bijection is the identity, so the induced basis map and renamed primitive list are unchanged.

For any N≥2 swap wires 0 and 1 while fixing the rest. Its induced P is involutive and nontrivial: the bitstring with bit 0 at wire 0 and bit 1 everywhere else changes under this swap. Output-only replacement U↦PU gives (PI)(PI)=P²=I for two identity stages, whereas output-only replacement after composition gives P(II)=P≠I. It therefore fails to preserve products.

An arbitrary computational-label permutation need not arise from wire renaming. On one wire the only wire bijection is identity and thus leaves RY(θ) unchanged; nevertheless the independent label swap X=[[0,1],[1,0]] obeys XRY(θ)X=RY(-θ). At θ=pi, RY(pi)=[[0,-1],[1,0]] and RY(-pi)=[[0,1],[-1,0]], so they differ. This is a counterexample to an unrelated-P wire-renaming claim, not to the algebraic validity of conjugation by arbitrary permutations. A nonzero angle alone is not sufficient for every such counterexample, which is why the specific angle is supplied.
